Berlin Dispatches: The world watches Canada as it stands up to Trump

Listen to audio version of this article
Sponsored by
0:00 / 4:11
Instaread

From alcohol bans to abandoned trips south, Canada’s response to Trump’s tariffs is reshaping its identity — and capturing Europe’s attention.

Aug. 30, 2026
Aug. 30, 2026

By Robert WilliamsReporter

Editor’s Note: This is the fourth in a series of weekly dispatches Robert Williams will send during his two months living and working in Berlin as part of the Arthur F. Burns Fellowship, an opportunity for mid-career journalists to get a taste of foreign correspondence.

These updates will offer a glimpse into the thoughts of a Canadian journalist finding his footing in a German newsroom and adapting to life in Berlin.

It is a strange sensation to read about your own country halfway across the world.

ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW

After I woke up Saturday in Berlin, I walked past a row of newsstands tucked between bakeries and tram stops, and there was Canada, suddenly front‑page news: the nation standing up to the United States and Donald Trump.

When I talk to Germans, conversations seem to bend toward Canada the moment someone learns where I’m from. There is a deep interest right now, a fascination with how a quiet country has found itself in a loud geopolitical moment.

The 30‑day countdown had just begun on the latest trade escalation when I arrived in late July, and while the deadline loomed heavy back home, it went largely unnoticed here. 

But once people asked about the tensions and I started talking about alcohol bans, buying local and our immense disinterest in comments about becoming a 51st state, it made Germans pause, eyebrows raised, as they began to understand the personal Canadian momentum behind our government’s hard stance against Trump and his repeated jabs at our sovereignty.

Then Prime Minister Mark Carney announced Canada was walking away from the trade deal in the eleventh hour last week, and suddenly our country was right back in the limelight.

I was asked to write an opinion piece at Die Zeit to try to explain to German readers the personal toll these tariffs take on Canadians. Here is an excerpt from the piece — translated into German for Die Zeit, then back into English for you:

ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW
ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW

“The need to differentiate ourselves from our southern neighbours has become something I carry with me, a quiet shift I only began to understand once I saw how deeply the tariff war has changed the way Canadians travel, shop, and even talk about the country next door. In that collective pulling back, Canada feels more reflective — a place rediscovering itself and what makes it a country worth standing up for.

“Canadians watching the tariff war unfold are reminded that this is a country whose innovations — from insulin and the cardiac pacemaker to the telephone and standard time zones — have quietly helped shape global stability and modern life.

“It’s bitterly ironic that a nation responsible for the Canadarm, peacekeeping, and even rescuing six Americans in Tehran during the Iran hostage crisis in 1979 now finds itself absorbing economic shocks from a neighbour whose prosperity has so often relied on Canadian partnership and ingenuity.

“When the wildfires ravaged Southern California last year, we sent firefighters and water bombers.

“When wildfires burned out of control across Canada this summer, we read social media posts from the American president threatening more tariffs.

“These are not moments that everyday Canadians will forget as they try to cancel out the noise of Trump as more factory floors go silent in their cities and towns.”

ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW
ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW

Cancelling out that noise has become more difficult since I wrote those words last weekend, with Trump now attempting to rename Lake Ontario as Lake America.

But perhaps a few comments on my story from German readers can give you some solace in the way this is viewed by those outside North America.

“Canada is and remains for me one of the most sympathetic countries on the planet. Big, wide, impressive and with people who meet you openly, friendly and amazingly unexcited. A fairly clear contrast to what you get a few thousand kilometres further south.”

“I wish the Canadians a lot of endurance and may they continue to remain consistent and united.”

“Thinking more globally: Canada as a member of the EU would be attractive for both sides!”

So, to everyone back home, stay strong through these difficult times.

The world is watching.
